# Doris "Dorie" Miller

Doris Miller (October 12, 1919 – November 24, 1943) was a significant American hero of World War II. Here is a comprehensive overview of what is known about him:

---

## Early Life

- Born in **Willow Springs, Texas**, near Waco, to Connery and Henrietta Miller
- He was the third of four sons
- Grew up working on his family's farm and played fullback on his high school football team
- He was known by the nickname **"Dorie"**

---

## Military Enlistment

- Enlisted in the **United States Navy** in September **1939** at age 19
- As was common for Black servicemen of the era due to racial segregation policies, he was assigned as a **Mess Attendant** (cook/steward), one of the few roles open to African Americans at the time
- He was assigned to the **USS West Virginia (BB-48)**

---

## Attack on Pearl Harbor – December 7, 1941

This is the defining moment of his story:

- When Japanese aircraft attacked Pearl Harbor, Miller was collecting laundry aboard the West Virginia
- He helped carry his **mortally wounded captain**, Mervyn Bennion, to safety
- Despite having **no formal training** on anti-aircraft weapons, he manned a **.50 caliber Browning anti-aircraft machine gun** and fired at Japanese aircraft
- Accounts suggest he may have **shot down several Japanese planes**, though the exact number was disputed
- He continued firing until he ran out of ammunition and was ordered to abandon ship
- He also helped rescue other wounded sailors

---

## Recognition and Awards

- He was awarded the **Navy Cross** on May 27, 1942, by Admiral Chester Nimitz — the Navy's third-highest honor at the time
- Nimitz praised him for his "distinguished devotion to duty, extraordinary courage and disregard for his own personal safety"
- There were significant public and political campaigns, particularly from the **Black press and civil rights organizations**, urging the government to award him the **Medal of Honor**, which he was ultimately denied, largely due to racial discrimination
- He became a **celebrated figure** and was used in **war bond recruitment posters** and campaigns, particularly targeting the African American community

---

## Continued Service and Death

- After Pearl Harbor, he served on the **USS Indianapolis** and later the **USS Liscome Bay**, an escort carrier
- On **November 24, 1943**, the USS Liscome Bay was struck by a torpedo from a Japanese submarine (**I-175**) near **Butaritari (Makin Atoll)** in the Pacific
- The ship sank rapidly after its bomb magazine exploded
- Miller was among the **more than 640 men killed** — he was **24 years old**
- His body was never recovered

---

## Legacy

- Miller became one of the **most celebrated African American heroes** of World War II
- His story was widely used to challenge racial segregation in the military
- He is credited as one of the figures who helped build momentum toward **President Truman's Executive Order 9981 (1948)**, which desegregated the U.S. military
- The **USS Miller (FF-1091)**, a Navy frigate, was named in his honor in 1973
- The **USS Doris Miller (CVN-81)**, a Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, was named after him — a landmark honor making him one of the few African Americans to have a major naval vessel named after them
- There are **monuments, schools, and buildings** named in his honor across the United States, particularly in Texas
- His likeness has appeared on **postage stamps** and in various memorials
- The **2019 film "Midway"** featured him as a character, and he also appeared in the **2001 film "Pearl Harbor"**
- There have been ongoing campaigns to **posthumously award him the Medal of Honor**

---

## Historical Significance

Miller's story is important beyond individual heroism — it highlights:
- The **contradiction of Black Americans fighting for a country that denied them equal rights**
- The role of the **Black press** (such as the Pittsburgh Courier) in publicizing his story
- The systemic **racial discrimination** in the U.S. military during WWII
- His legacy as a symbol of **Black patriotism and valor**

---

He remains one of the most important and honored figures from the Pearl Harbor attack and World War II in general.
